background.definition: Rhabdomyolysis is disintegration or dissolution of striated muscle, which leads to highly elevated levels of muscle enzymes in the blood stream and can in some cases lead to renal failure. Most studies define it as a CK 5 times the upper limit of normal.

list.listitem: 26,000 cases in U.S. per year
0.44 cases per 10,000 person years for monotherapy with atorvastatin, pravastatin, or simvastatin (95% CI, 0.20-0.84)
5.34 cases per 10,000 person years for cervistatin (95% CI, 1.46-13.68)
5.98 cases per 10,000 person years for combination therapy of statin plus fibrate (95% CI, 0.72-216.0)
1035 cases per 10,000 person years for cervistatin plus fibrate (95% CI, 389-2117)
No comprehensive data are available on prevalence of rhabdomyolysis.
The number needed to treat to harm (NNTH) for 5 years with statin monotherapy to observe 1 case of rhabdomyolysis is 5680.

Sixty percent of cases of statin-related rhabdomyolysis are attributed to drug-drug interactions. Drug-drug interactions commonly causing rhabdomyolysis include statin+fibrates, cyclosporines, macrolide antibiotics, warfarin, or digoxin.
The frequency of statin induced rhabdomyolysis is <0.1%. However, 10% of patients stop their statins due to muscle complaints even though evidence does not show that statins are the cause.

A systematic review of case reports and case series identified 43 publications with 345 individuals with exertional rhabomyolysis, of whom 16% developed acute kidney injury (AKI). Almost all with AKI (97%) were ultraendurance runners.
Of these, the three most likely causes are trauma, immobilization, and sepsis.
Alcohol abuse (especially intoxication with immobilization).
Muscle overexertion or compression.

Medications (statins). A network meta-analysis identified 24 RCTs of statins to evaluate the association between statin dose and muscle problems. Compared to moderate intensity statins, high intensity statins were more likely to be associated. with any muscle problem (RR 1.04, 95% CI, 1.0-1.07, I2 = 0%), myalgia (RR 1.04, 95% CI, 1.0-1.08, I2 = 0%, NNH = 173), leaving the study due to muscle problems (RR 1.37, 95% CI, 1.09-1.73, I2 = 0%, NNH = 218), and elevated creatine kinase (RR 5.4, 95% CI, 2.5-11.6, I2 = 7%, NNH = 589).
Illicit drugs (cocaine).
Hyperthermia: malignant hyperthermia, neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Metabolic disorders: hyperosmolar coma, ketoacidosis, hypokalemia.
Toxins: snake and insect venom, carbon monoxide, mushroom poisoning.
Myopathy: congenital muscle enzyme deficiency.

Muscle injury results in cascade of events that leads to leakage of calcium ions into the intracellular space, causing a pathologic interaction between actin and myosin, leading to muscle destruction.
Muscle damage leads to release of muscle breakdown products, notably myoglobin and muscle enzymes into the plasma.

The classic triad of rhabdomyolysis consists of myalgias, generalized weakness, and darkened urine; however, only 50% of patients present with this triad. C
Serum CK >5 times the upper limit of normal is the most sensitive indicator. C
The classic triad of rhabdomyolysis consists of myalgias, generalized weakness, and darkened urine; however, only 50% of patients present with this triad.
Most frequently involved muscles are generally proximal muscles such as shoulders, thighs, calves and lower back.
General manifestations include malaise, fever, tachycardia, nausea, and vomiting.
In most cases, the history reflects an inciting cause, such as alcohol use and unresponsiveness, agitation, illicit drug use, polypharmacy, or heat stroke.
Physical signs that should alert physicians to the possibility of rhabdomyolysis are pressure necrosis of skin, multiple trauma or crush injury, increased muscle tone.
Physical exam may demonstrate muscle rigidity, muscle weakness, muscle swelling and tenderness, fevers, and/or vomiting.
Pain with passive movement is associated with compartment syndrome.

Adult Treatment Panel III Guidelines recommend that a baseline CK measurements should be obtained upon starting statin therapy. Obtain a CK measurement if patient reports muscle symptoms suggestive of rhabdomyolysis and compare to baseline CK measurement. However, the usefulness of routine baseline CK measurement and frequent CK monitoring on patients on statins has been debated, and the evidence is inconclusive but it may be helpful.
Serum CK >5 times the upper limit of normal is most sensitive indicator.
Plasma myoglobin measurements are not reliable because the half-life of myoglobin is 1 to 3 hours, and myoglobin is cleared within 6 hours.
Urine myoglobin is presumed if the urine is positive for blood but negative for red blood cells.
Hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, or hypocalcemia may be associated with rhabdomyolysis.
See algorithm in for recommended approach to the patient with rhabdomyolysis.
Aggressive IV hydration to ensure urine output of 300 cc/hour is the cornerstone of treatment. C
Available evidence suggests that mannitol and bicarbonate have no benefit over aggressive fluid resuscitation. B

Guidelines for the prevention of acute kidney injury (AKI) in patients with rhabdomyolysis was developed by the Danish Society of Intensive Care Medicine (DSIT) and the Danish Society of Anesthesia and Intensive Care Medicine (DASAIM). They emphasize the overall low quality of evidence. Specific recommendations include using early fluid resuscitation with crystalloids over late resuscitation or use of colloids. They also recommend against the routine use of loop diuretics or mannitol.

A guideline from the Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma identified 12 studies to inform their guideline. They recommend aggressive IV fluid resuscitation as the cornerstone of therapy to reduce the incidence of acute renal failure (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.14-0.77) but based on only 2 studies with 64 patients. Aggressive IV fluids also reduced the risk of dialysis (RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.06-0.72) based on 3 studies with 106 patients. Bicarbonate did not reduce the incidence of acute renal failure (5 studies) or dialysis (4 studies). Mannitol similarl did not reduce the inidence of acute renal failure (3 studies) or dialysis (2 studies).

Aggressive IV hydration to ensure urine output of 250 to 300 cc/hour is the cornerstone of therapy. Based on expert opinion and limited trial data fluids should be administered at 400 ml/hour or 4 to 8 liters/day, adjusted based on urine output. One small study found a benefit to LR over normal saline but no clinical outcomes were reported in the study.
A systematic review of case series and case reports of exertional rhabdomyolysis in athletes found that most commonly they gave early IV fluid replacement at a rate of 400 ml/hour.

Urine alkalinization with bicarbonate infusion has traditionally been recommended, as well as diuresis with furosemide. Available evidence suggests that mannitol and bicarbonate have no benefit over aggressive fluid resuscitation although studies are limited.
Danish guidelines (2019) also recommend against urine alkalinization and use of mannitol.

Renal replacment therapy (RRT) when indicated in consultation with nephrology. A recent study developed a model to predict when RRT may be indicated. However, a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the efficacy of continuous RRT (CRRT) over standard care and prevention of AKI due to rhabdomyolysis.
If compartment syndrome is present, fasciotomy may be indicated.
Treat until serum CK plateaus and begins to fall; serum creatinine is consistently below 1.7 mg/dl; and potassium, phosphate, and uric acid are within normal limits.
Patient may be discharged when above criteria met and able to orally hydrate.
Patient may gradually return to activity once CK <700, serum creatinine <1.4 mg/dl, and symptom free.
In the absence of signs of nephrotoxicity, urinary casts/cells, urinary myoglobin, or metabolic abnormalities, patients may be treated as outpatients.
Any patient with elevated potassium, phosphate, or uric acid levels should be hospitalized.
Admission to the ICU should be considered in elderly patients or those with comorbid cardiovascular disease or preexisting renal dysfunction.
Patients with CK >5-10 times the upper limit of normal are usually admitted to hospital.
Compartment syndrome: orthopedics consultation
Renal failure: nephrology consultation
Hyperkalemia: give kayexalate
Best predictors of acute renal failure (ARF) are elevated serum creatinine and BUN; in a series of 100, no ARF if serum creatinine <1.7 mg/dL. B
Prognosis is good even in cases where renal failure has developed. C
If discharged from hospitalized with CKs that are above normal limit, patient should be checked for serum CK every 24 to 72 hours until in normal range. C
Older patients are at higher risk.
May consider admission to ICU in older patients with coexisting cardiac or existing renal disease.
